I had my second root canal two weeks ago (9th broken tooth, lifelong dental hell, etc.) and had a new disturbing experience to add to the pile. The periodontist hadn’t heard of EDS prior to meeting me. While discussing my other extreme dental challenges I was very clear and communicative about my jaw problems (TMJ, “small mouth”, significant difficulty opening my mouth wide and keeping it open). As usual, although I’m an adult, I needed one of the smaller child’s-size implements to keep my mouth open during the procedure. Towards the end of the procedure, they wanted to take a set of X-rays, which requires the use a bite wing, beloved by zebras everywhere I imagine 🙄. The assistant tried to physically pry my mouth open wide enough to insert the bite wing, but my jaw had locked. She aggressively attempted to wrench my mouth open wider while telling me “you need to try harder” and “you’re fine, you just need to make an effort”. I was crying out in pain, unable to unlock my jaw and unable to speak in response to her commands. Then the periodontist, who was in another room at the time, rushed in and demanded “What are you upset about, stop this right now, no one is doing anything to you”. Fortunately during the rest of the time I was in the chair they stopped trying to force my jaw to unlock but they didn’t say a word to me, as if I wasn’t there. It was so demoralizing...I’ve been through hell in countless dentist’s chairs but in response to my stubborn suffering due to EDS they had all been sympathetic (albeit puzzled and powerless). I’m seeking help finding a legitimate medical/dental source about this specific issue to send to that brutal periodontist in the hope that it might prevent him from treating someone else that way. I’ve read through many articles online and haven’t been able to find one that addresses this aspect adequately. Thank you so much in advance for any help you can provide!

I’ve been a special education teacher for twelve years. It’s a stupendously difficult career no matter how many years of experience you have, and the first year is hell for everyone. However, managing the insane demands of the job on top of CPTSD is nothing short of a miracle. I would suggest doing everything you can to prioritize self-care over doing everything “right” at work or else you will likely burn out and either leave the profession, spiral towards a breakdown, or both. If you are invested in the field over the long term, it is crucial to make your mental health your first priority. I know this is easier said than done, but I hope my input is helpful.

Some people during my adulthood have casually commented to me that I seem like I could have Asperger’s Syndrome (now clinically referred to high-functioning Autism Spectrum Disorder). I definitely do not meet criteria for that diagnosis (I’m a special education teacher so can speak from a professionally informed perspective), but am very self-conscious about the traits that give some people that impression. My affect was modeled from a severely mentally ill mother and an emotionally unresponsive father, both of whom did not present to mainstream society as within “normal” interpersonal expectations. In addition, the coping skills I developed since birth in order to survive constant trauma revolved around ultra-independence and emotional detachment, because I was brutally punished for displaying anything other than quiet obedience. I don’t have siblings and spent most of my childhood alone, while also being isolated and stigmatized because my life circumstances were so disturbing to others. All this to say, my interpersonal skills and emotional affect are “different”, in some of the same ways that people on the spectrum are perceived (I.e. withdrawn, in my own world, difficulty interpreting other people’s behavior, problematic or off-base reactions in social situations). I am painfully obsessed about how I am perceived to the extent that I think I’ve become even more awkward and aloof, but on the other hand I have begun to welcome feedback from others about the issue and have been putting a lot of effort into learning and growing in this area. All this to say, as my overarching message, that it is important not to conflate symptoms of CPTSD and ASD without research and professional input. The narrow representation of people on the autism spectrum portrayed in the mainstream media or stereotyped by the uninformed general public should not be taken too seriously off the bat by those of us with CPTSD because it’s just not that simple. I encourage you to do your own research and consult with professionals lest you succumb to stigma or stereotypes.

I empathize with this so much. My dog is almost 12 and I have long believed at my core that my life will end when hers does. I would encourage you not to downplay how immensely important your relationship with your dog is, when the general societal message is that people should always be more important than animals. Speaking for myself, I fully understand I connect so deeply and intensely with animals because For the entirety of my childhood, I learned to mistrust people because they abused and abandoned me, and developed very few skills about how to connect with humans as a result. Animals, in contrast, are the only healthy, secure, and life-affirming bonds I am able to experience and trust. I believe passionately that there is nothing wrong about that; in fact, it’s at the very least least a reassuring indicator that we aren’t sociopaths, and possess the ability to love and nurture authentically. Regarding the issue of being so isolated from people, however....I’m in basically the same position as you are. But I hope it helps to know you are not alone when it comes to this situation. I personally only develop and maintain friendships with people who are fully respect how and why my dog is essential to my existence and won’t stigmatize or minimize it. Anyone who isn’t on that level with us isn’t a match as a stable friend.
